title: El Moro Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: See El Moro well depths, yields, water levels, drilling costs, and nearby permit history. The median well depth is 56 feet.
h1: El Moro, Colorado Well Depths, Yields, and Costs
intro_html:
Buying land near El Moro means evaluating more than the presence of a well permit. Records within five miles show a median completed depth of 56 feet, but the middle half runs from 40 to 150 feet. Reported well yields have a median of 11.0 gallons per minute, although only 12 wells report a pump yield.

This area is plains country with alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. The records include Hoehne and Trinidad nearby, and they show both shallow wells and much deeper exceptions. Use these figures to frame a driller's estimate, not to guarantee what a new hole will find.

sections.heading: What well depth looks like around El Moro
sections.html:
El Moro wells are commonly shallow compared with many mountain and fractured-granite areas. The median recorded depth is 56 feet, and the middle half of wells falls between 40 and 150 feet. About 62% are under 100 feet, while 26% fall from 100 to 300 feet.

There are deeper exceptions. The 90th percentile is 300 feet, and the deepest recorded well reaches 780 feet. For a drilling bid, that spread matters: a shallow estimate may fit much of the local record, but your lot can still require substantially more footage based on the local formation, water-bearing zones, casing, and the driller's experience near the property.

sections.heading: Expected well yield on the El Moro plains
sections.html:
Reported yields are generally useful, but the data set is limited because only 12 permits report a pump yield. Among those records, the median is 11.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 6.5 and 15.0 gallons per minute.

The yield mix is encouraging for many domestic buyers: 50% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 33% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Still, 8% are under 1 gallon per minute, and another 8% are from 1 to 5 gallons per minute. Ask for the well-completion report and a current pump test before assuming a stock, irrigation, or larger household supply is adequate.

sections.heading: Water levels and what the records can tell you
sections.html:
The available static-water data show a median depth to water of 34 feet, with the middle half from 26 to 42 feet. That is useful when estimating pump placement and evaluating an existing well, but only 2 wells report a static water level.

Because the sample is so small, it does not establish a reliable water-table trend for El Moro. The permit history also does not provide enough static measurements by decade to conclude that the water table is falling or stable. Have the current owner document the water level, pump performance, and recovery behavior. A driller can compare those observations with nearby wells in El Moro, Hoehne, and Trinidad.

sections.heading: Permit history and drillers active near El Moro
sections.html:
The local record is long but uneven. Permits were issued from the 1950s through the 2020s, with the newest permit dated 2025. The largest groups are from the 1990s, with 46 permits, and the 2000s, with 41. There are 153 wells in the surrounding permit records, while 87 are recorded as constructed and 93 report a total depth.

Boday Well Drilling appears most often, listed under Boday, Alex with 32 records and Boday, Kathleen with 19. Authorized (Pe, Pg) appears on 10. These names describe permit history, not a recommendation. Before hiring, confirm current licensing, insurance, availability, and experience at your exact site.

sections.heading: What drilling a new well may cost at El Moro
sections.html:
For local alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the drilling model uses about $35 to $55 per foot. At the median depth of 56 feet, the drilled hole alone models at approximately $2,000 to $3,100. That is not the complete water system.

A finished well including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $8,000 to $15,100 at that median depth. A deeper hole, difficult access, additional casing or grout, or challenging electrical and trench work can move the bid beyond that range. Get a written scope that separates footage, casing, development, pump equipment, testing, trenching, and electrical work.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying or building
sections.html:
Low yield and dry-hole risk remain important even though the reported median yield is 11.0 gallons per minute. The records include 8% of wells under 1 gallon per minute, and reported yields exist for only 12 wells. Confirm the actual well's production, storage capacity, recovery, and water quality instead of relying only on nearby averages.

Environmental review also matters. Within about ten miles, the map shows 13 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 164 historic mine features, with 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test existing water and locate septic systems, replacement areas, driveways, and building envelopes before construction. Colorado DWR permits and exempt household-use rules control what the well may legally serve; over-appropriated basins may require an augmentation plan.

sections.heading: A practical plan for an El Moro lot
sections.html:
Start with the DWR permit, well construction report, pump information, and a current water test. Confirm the recorded depth against the actual casing and pump setup, then compare the property with nearby wells rather than using a countywide assumption. The local aquifer labels are mostly unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with 148 wells in that category; 4 name Pierre Shale and 1 names Denver.

For a new build, have the driller, septic designer, and excavator review the lot together. Plan access for the rig, protect well and septic separation, and verify the legal use before designing irrigation or stock facilities. A well can make adequate water and still require careful storage, treatment, electrical, and seasonal management.

faq.q: How deep are wells in El Moro, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth within five miles of El Moro is 56 feet. The middle half runs from 40 to 150 feet. About 62% are under 100 feet, but the deepest recorded well is 780 feet, so nearby records cannot guarantee the depth at a specific lot.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in El Moro?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the median depth of 56 feet, the drilled hole is estimated at about $2,000 to $3,100. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at approximately $8,000 to $15,100.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce near El Moro?
faq.a: Among the 12 local records reporting pump yield, the median is 11.0 gallons per minute, with a middle half from 6.5 to 15.0 gallons per minute. However, 8% report under 1 gallon per minute. Require a pump test before relying on a well for household, stock, or irrigation use.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in El Moro?
faq.a: A permit or nearby well yield does not establish drinking-water safety. Test the property’s water for normal domestic concerns and site-specific contaminants. The mapped area includes 13 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 164 historic mine features within about ten miles, so review local conditions and test before using the water for drinking.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near El Moro?
faq.a: The available records do not show a reliable trend. Only 2 wells report static water levels, with a median depth to water of 34 feet and a middle half from 26 to 42 feet. That sample is too small to establish a falling or stable water table. Check current levels and well recovery at the property.
